title: Gideon, the Least in His Family
lead: God sees potential where we see only our own weakness.
questions: What list of your own shortcomings do you keep reciting to God, and what would happen if He stopped listening to it and started sending you?
Whom in your church could you call a “mighty man of valor” ahead of time, and so help that person out of the winepress?
What altar do you need to deal with first in your own backyard before God sends you any farther?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: After seven years under the Midianites, Israel was living in its own land like strangers, hiding its harvest in caves. We meet Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress, a pit cut into the rock, out of sight. And to this man the angel of the LORD says: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” God has a habit of naming people not for who they are at the moment but for who they are meant to become. Gideon’s reply is bitter and honest: if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? “And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us…?” He knew the exodus secondhand. What he knew firsthand was Midian. God didn’t answer with a lecture. He said only: “Go in the strength you have… Am I not sending you?” And when Gideon protested that he was the youngest in the weakest clan, he got the same answer Moses got at the burning bush: “I will be with you.”

His first assignment wasn’t a battle. It was housecleaning in his father’s yard: tear down the family altar to Baal. Gideon did it at night, “because he was too afraid.” Obedience with fear inside is still obedience. Then he asked for signs with the fleece, and God answered both tests without a word of reproach. He would rather do that than lose a man who is afraid to ask. And before the battle something remarkable happened: the commander was told he had too many soldiers, because Israel might say, “My own hand has saved me.” Of thirty-two thousand, three hundred remained, too few for anyone to credit the victory to a man. On the night of the battle God added: “If you are afraid… go down to the camp with your servant Purah,” and He let Gideon overhear an enemy’s dream about a loaf of barley bread that knocks a tent flat. The battle was won by horns, torches and three hundred shattered jars in God’s service: light hidden in clay that shone out when the jar broke. After the victory Gideon humbly turned down the crown: “The LORD shall rule over you.”

This story is for everyone who answers God’s call with a list of shortcomings. God doesn’t argue with that way of thinking. He finds people in the winepress and greets them by a name they haven’t grown into yet.

The time of the judges is a vicious circle: turning away from God, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and then all over again. This time the hard years had already lasted seven, and they had a name: Midian. The Midianites were so ruthless that “the Israelites prepared shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds.” The people who had entered the Promised Land under Joshua were now living there like foreigners, hiding their harvest in caves. We close this section on faith in the minority with a story in which being few is not an accident but God’s design: out of thirty-two thousand soldiers, the Lord will leave three hundred.

sections.heading: Mighty Man of Valor
paragraphs: We meet Gideon in a winepress, threshing wheat. That one sentence is a portrait of the age. You don’t thresh grain in a winepress. You thresh it on an open threshing floor, in the wind. Gideon is threshing in a pit hewn out of rock, in hiding, so the Midianites won’t take his grain. And to this man, tucked away in a hole with a handful of wheat, the angel of the LORD says: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.” It’s hard to imagine a wider gap between a greeting and the situation it finds. But God has a habit of naming people not for who they are at the moment but for who they are meant to become. He will call Simon the Rock (Petros / Kephas) long before Simon stops cracking. Gideon’s answer is bitter and honest: “Please, my Lord… if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us…?” Every generation knows that question: the one raised on stories of God’s great acts in the past, now looking around at its own reality. Gideon knows the exodus secondhand. What he knows firsthand is Midian. And it is to this embittered man that the Lord entrusts the next chapter of His wonders.

sections.heading: Go in the Strength You Have
paragraphs: God’s answer is not a lecture on suffering: “Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?” In the strength you have. Not: go once you’ve grown. Gideon objects exactly the way Moses defended himself at the bush: “How can I save Israel? Indeed, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.” The two calls are built on the same pattern: both men are hiding from the enemy, both ask “who am I,” both hear the same answer. Because here too God doesn’t correct the man’s self-assessment by a single word. He doesn’t say: you’re exaggerating, you’re stronger than you think. He says: “Surely I will be with you… and you will strike down all the Midianites as one man.” That answer comes back in Scripture every time a task is too big for a person, because every time the truth is the same: the outcome isn’t decided by the size of the one sent but by the presence of the One who sends.

sections.heading: First, the Altar at Home
paragraphs: Gideon’s first assignment isn’t at the front. It’s in his father’s yard: tear down the family altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole. Before anyone delivers a nation, he has to deal with the idol in his own house, and that is an order God still keeps today. After that night Gideon was given the nickname Jerubbaal, “Let Baal contend with him.” An interesting find from archaeology: on a fragment of a clay jar from the period of the judges, found in the Shephelah, the rare name Jerubbaal was written. It doesn’t prove that Gideon himself existed, but it’s welcome news for the reader: the names in this story belong to its own world, not to a legend written centuries later. And the narrator adds a detail that makes you love this book: Gideon did as the LORD had told him, “but because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city, he did it by night rather than in the daytime.” He did it afraid. Obedience with fear inside is still obedience. God didn’t wait for Gideon’s hands to stop shaking. It was enough that those frightened hands took the altar apart. Courage in the Bible is seldom the absence of fear. Most often it’s doing the right thing in spite of fear.

sections.heading: The Fleece
paragraphs: Before the battle Gideon asks for a sign, and he asks twice: first let the dew be only on the fleece and the ground dry, then the other way around. He senses he’s pushing it, because he opens the second request with: “Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time.” God answers both tests without a word of reproach. This scene is often read as a model for discerning God’s will, but in the text it’s something else. Gideon isn’t looking for the Lord’s will. He already knows it; he heard it plainly. He’s simply gathering the courage to believe it. The fleece is not a pattern for prayer here. It’s a witness to God’s patience with a faith that needs more reassurance than it should. The Creator would rather answer an extra question than lose a man who is afraid to ask.

sections.heading: Too Many Soldiers
paragraphs: Then comes an extraordinary briefing, in which the commander is told he has too many soldiers. “You have too many people for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” The first cut: whoever is afraid may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand remain. The second cut, this time at the water: three hundred remain. Facing them is an enemy “like a swarm of locusts,” with camels “as countless as the sand on the seashore.” The Lord deliberately trims the resources down to the point where the victory can’t be credited to anything but Him. That is a very uncomfortable truth for everyone who measures God’s chances by human strength, in the church too: our weakness is sometimes exactly what the Lord needs so that His strength can be seen. Three hundred men could not win this fight. It was a group too small for anyone to credit the victory to a man. One thing is worth watching here: the text never says the three hundred were chosen because they drank more alertly or more wisely. The criterion stays unexplained, probably on purpose, so that no one would turn it into a method for recruiting the best. God wasn’t assembling an elite. He kept counting people off until there were so few that all the glory could go only to Him.

sections.heading: If You’re Afraid, Take Purah
paragraphs: The night before the battle brings one of the warmest sayings in this book. God says: “Get up and go down against the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand. But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah.” If you are afraid. God knows Gideon is still afraid, after all the signs, after the fleece, after the army was cut down, and He doesn’t scold him for it. He gives him a companion and a concrete way to find courage. Down in the enemy camp, Gideon overhears one Midianite telling another a dream about a loaf of barley bread that came tumbling into the camp and overturned a tent. Barley bread was the bread of the poor, the food of people whose wheat had been taken. The enemy interpreted the dream himself: “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon.” The commander heard about his victory from his opponent’s own lips, and he worshiped the Lord right there. Sometimes God encourages His people in the strangest way imaginable: He lets them hear that the other side is more afraid.

sections.heading: Jars and Torches
paragraphs: The battle itself is an anti-battle. Three hundred men surround the camp at night, each with a horn in one hand and a clay jar with a torch hidden inside it in the other. At the signal they smash the jars, raise the torches, blow the horns and shout: “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” Not one of them has a hand free for a sword. Light, noise and panic do all the work: in the darkness the enemy soldiers take each other for the attackers. There is more in this picture than a clever stratagem: light shut up in a clay vessel that begins to shine only when the vessel breaks. Centuries later Paul would write that “we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” That night near Harod we see three hundred broken jars and a battle won by light.

sections.heading: The LORD Shall Rule
paragraphs: After the victory Israel makes Gideon the kind of offer many a victor’s heart has waited for: “Rule over us—you and your son and grandson.” A dynasty. Gideon’s answer is the last sentence of this section and its summary: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you.” The man who started out as the least in his family, down in the hole of a winepress, ends by refusing the crown. Maybe that’s exactly why God chooses the small: people who remember where the Lord found them are less likely to mistake His throne for their own.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This story is for everyone who answers God’s call with a list of their own shortcomings: the church is too small, the gifts too weak, the age too late, the life story all wrong. God doesn’t argue with that way of thinking. He simply ignores it, and sometimes He even deepens the shortage, so that the success can be credited to Him alone. And one more important thing about how we look at one another: the angel found Gideon down in a pit, in hiding, at the least heroic moment of his life, and greeted him with the words “mighty man of valor.” That is how God looks at people: ahead of time, seeing who they can become. If in our churches we looked at each other even a little with those eyes, many a Gideon would come out of the winepress sooner.
